title: Programmable solids that become different load-bearing mechanisms

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reusable structural object whose mechanical function can be rewritten by reversibly changing its internal connections or stiffness. The same constituent hardware could form a rigid beam in one configuration and a mechanism with controlled motion in another. The defining capability is to change which motions the object permits and how it carries working loads, while retaining useful structural performance.

Conceptual synthesis: An initial realization could switch between a load-bearing beam and a useful one-degree-of-freedom mechanism, meaning a mechanism with one independently controlled motion. Hinges, grippers and transmissions describe a broader possible repertoire, each requiring an appropriate mechanical design. Connectivity-changing modular lattices are one route; stiffness-changing or compliant structures are other possible routes and need not use the same reversible joints or communication architecture.

significance.text: If achieved reliably, this capability would let machines change mechanical function while reusing their structural hardware. Reconfiguration could alter load paths and permitted motion, allowing one object to serve different mechanical roles. The 2024 work by Gregg and colleagues supplies a relevant technical foundation through robotic lattice reconfiguration and the aim of adapting structural properties and form, but does not establish this broader mechanism-changing capability.

Conditional engineering synthesis: A successful beam-to-mechanism transformation would establish an initial instance of reusable mechanical functionality. A wider repertoire could support machines that change tasks without exchanging entire mechanical assemblies, or equipment that alternates between a stiff supporting state and a moving working state. Such benefits would depend on transformation time, energy use, reliability, payload capacity and the mass of supporting equipment. Grippers and transmissions would additionally require suitable geometry, actuation, interfaces and control.

Interpretive limit: Programmability would remain bounded by the object's available parts, geometry, connection rules, materials and actuators. A two-state demonstration would not establish arbitrary shape conversion or universal mechanical functionality. Likewise, an ultralight lattice with favorable performance relative to its mass should not be equated with a dense solid having metal-like assembled strength; those are different engineering achievements.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is repeatable integration of reversible functional change with useful load-bearing performance in the same object. For autonomous modular systems that change connectivity, structural connections, actuation, power and control must work together. The reviewed manuscript identifies inadequate connection strength and the mass penalties of integrated coupling, actuation or bonding as limitations on assembled strength and stiffness. These requirements apply to that architectural class; reversible connections and intermodule communication are not universal requirements for every stiffness-changing or compliant solid.

Engineering synthesis: Connections must hold loads with sufficient stiffness, release when commanded, reconnect accurately and retain their performance after repeated use. The object also needs a feasible transformation sequence: changing a connection can remove a load path or introduce unwanted motion before the next configuration is secured. Depending on the application, transformation may therefore require unloading, temporary support or coordinated actuation. Whether working loads must remain supported during transformation is an additional requirement to specify.

The precursor separates actuation from structural components to pursue efficient structural performance relative to system mass. That is a useful architectural response to integration penalties, but leaves a system-level question for the proposed innovation: how much power, robotics, control and supporting hardware is required to obtain a particular reconfigurable function? The unsolved engineering task includes preserving strength and stiffness after cycling while providing deliberate motion in the mechanism state.

current_state.text: In 2024, Christine E. Gregg, Damiana Catanoso, Olivia Irene B. Formoso and colleagues reported “Ultralight, strong, and self-reprogrammable mechanical metamaterials” in Science Robotics. The supplied review describes a robotic structural system using a composite lattice, including a 256-voxel assembly and a separate disassembly-and-reconfiguration demonstration. A fastening robot could unbolt connections so that a transport robot could remove a voxel, relocate it and support its reattachment. This establishes robotic assembly and reversible lattice reconfiguration as relevant precursors.

The manuscript reports assembled compressive strength of 11.17 kPa and a modulus of 1.1129 MPa at a lattice density of approximately 0.0103 g/cm³. Supplementary Table S7 gives a slightly different mean compressive strength, 11.38 kPa, and identifies the modulus as a chord modulus; Table S8 gives voxel density as 0.010285 g/cm³. The strength discrepancy remains unresolved. These are ultralight assembled-lattice measurements, distinct from the much higher constituent coupon strengths reported elsewhere in the supplement. Favorable specific performance does not imply metal-like strength per unit assembled cross-sectional area.

The mechanical tests used separately hand-assembled specimens, including 3 × 3 × 3 voxel assemblies. Their measured properties should therefore not be presented as measurements taken during autonomous transformation. Supporting hardware also matters: in the 256-voxel build, two SOLL-E robots used tethered power, MMIC-I used batteries, and the system received wireless commands from a centralized controller. The reported experiments do not establish repeated in-place conversion of one object between a beam and a useful mechanism, nor do they demonstrate a dense solid with metal-like assembled strength.

The initial research check had access to the NASA abstract while the journal full text was inaccessible. The later supplied review used complete retained text from the 29-page manuscript and 19-page supplement, with document identity verified and no extraction truncation reported. Figures and movies were not visually inspected, so the account here rests on the reviewed prose and extracted tables. The supplied material documents the 2024 result but contains no freshness search establishing the field's frontier as of November 1, 2026; it therefore cannot establish whether subsequent work has closed the remaining gap.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: Use one object at least 0.1 m across that autonomously and reversibly switches between a load-bearing beam and a useful one-degree-of-freedom mechanism for 100 complete round trips. Define each round trip as beam-to-mechanism-to-beam. Specify useful mechanism motion, travel, allowable deflection, loading modes, boundary conditions and failure criteria before testing. These dimensions and cycle counts are proposed engineering thresholds, not established standards or results reported by the precursor study.
completion_criteria.label: A ≥0.1-m object autonomously completes 100 beam–mechanism round trips

completion_criteria.text: Proposed mechanical qualification: In each state, sustain at least 10 MPa nominal stress over a predefined load-bearing section under the specified working load. Report both net material area and gross envelope area, identify the area used for the nominal-stress threshold, and provide the corresponding stress under the other convention. This prevents a small selected material area from obscuring weak assembled performance. Report stiffness in the intended constrained directions and resistance to motion in the intended moving direction, together with useful travel and load capacity. A mechanism's permitted motion must be evaluated separately from unwanted compliance.
completion_criteria.label: Both states sustain ≥10 MPa with explicit stress-area accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed repeatability and reproducibility evidence: Measure stiffness and strength retention after cycling, document connection damage and fatigue observations, and disclose failed transformations as well as successful ones. Account for all power supplies, actuators, robots, controllers, fixtures and human interventions, including interventions needed to recover from faults. Provide sufficient geometry, material, assembly, control and test information for independent reproduction, and demonstrate repeatability across multiple specimens. One hundred round trips would provide a repeatability screen, not a general fatigue-life qualification.
completion_criteria.label: Multi-specimen cycling demonstrates repeatability with full resource and reproducibility accounting

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries: Report transformation time and energy, total system mass, environmental conditions, and whether the object must be unloaded or externally supported during reconfiguration. If load support during transformation is claimed, test that capability explicitly. Success would establish the demonstrated functions and operating envelope; additional mechanisms, load directions, scales or environments would require further evidence. Finite testing can establish demonstrated breadth and reliability within stated conditions, not literal universality.
completion_criteria.label: Transformation time, energy, and demonstrated operating envelope are reported

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: MEC-08, “Distributed actuators that simultaneously match skeletal muscle,” overlaps through the provision of force and motion. Such actuators could help drive reconfiguration or operate a resulting mechanism. MEC-05 additionally concerns how structural connectivity, stiffness and permitted motion change to create different load-bearing functions. The supplied title alone does not establish whether a particular MEC-08 architecture would also provide that capability.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-10, “Stress-directed growth of load-bearing structures,” overlaps through adaptation of structure and load paths. Its title emphasizes growth directed by stress, while MEC-05 emphasizes reversible rewriting of an existing object's mechanical function. Growth might enable or complement reconfiguration, but neither reversibility nor conversion between mechanism types follows from the supplied MEC-10 title. Their exact architectural boundaries remain unresolved.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-13, “General-purpose synthesis of practical mechanisms,” concerns the design problem of obtaining mechanisms that perform desired functions. MEC-05 concerns physical hardware that can change between such functions. Mechanism synthesis could supply target configurations and transformation constraints, but a successful design method would not by itself demonstrate a reusable material system capable of realizing those configurations.

Roster-based synthesis: MEC-04, “Ambient fatigue immunity in bulk structural metals,” and MEC-07, “Bulk structural solids at a large fraction of ideal strength,” address durability and strength that could benefit reconfigurable hardware. MEC-05 additionally requires reversible functional change and assembled-system performance. Strong constituents or fatigue-resistant materials would not alone establish reliable reconfigurable connections, while MEC-05's proposed 100-round-trip test would not establish fatigue immunity.

change_log.change: Preserved MEC-05's identity and explained the innovation as reversible rewriting of mechanical function through connectivity or stiffness changes.
change_log.reason: The central concept remains meaningful despite limits in the evidence for particular implementations and broader mechanism repertoires.

change_log.change: Scoped reversible connections, communication and associated integration requirements to relevant modular architectures.
change_log.reason: Stiffness-changing and compliant structures do not universally require the same connections or communication systems.

change_log.change: Separated the immediate beam-to-mechanism capability from conditional extensions to grippers, hinges and transmissions.
change_log.reason: Broader functions require additional geometry, actuation, interfaces and control; a two-state demonstration would not establish universal functionality.

change_log.change: Expanded the 2024 precursor account with the 256-voxel build, separate reconfiguration experiment, supporting power and control architecture, and hand-assembled mechanical test specimens.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish demonstrated robotic lattice reconfiguration from an integrated, repeatedly transforming load-bearing mechanism.

change_log.change: Added assembled strength, modulus and density, retained both reported strength values, and distinguished lattice measurements from constituent properties.
change_log.reason: The quantitative evidence supports an ultralight structural precursor without establishing dense, metal-like assembled strength; the main-text and supplementary strength values differ.

change_log.change: Updated the access account to include the later review's complete retained manuscript and supplement text while preserving the lack of visual inspection.
change_log.reason: The earlier abstract-only limitation no longer describes all supplied evidence, but figures and movies were not inspected.

change_log.change: Made the proposed demonstration reproducible through round-trip counting, stress-area conventions, motion criteria, stiffness retention, hardware accounting and operating boundaries.
change_log.reason: The original thresholds could otherwise leave cycle counting, assembled performance and useful mechanism behavior ambiguous.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster titles to explain qualified relationships with MEC-08 and MEC-10, and added direct design and material relationships with MEC-13, MEC-04 and MEC-07.
change_log.reason: The roster supports title-level distinctions but does not justify categorical claims about the full capabilities of those concepts.

change_log.change: Retained an explicit limit on field freshness and on the meaning of finite cycling tests.
change_log.reason: No freshness search was supplied, and 100 cycles cannot establish general fatigue life or universal mechanism conversion.

unresolved_issues: The cause of the difference between the manuscript's 11.17 kPa assembled compressive strength and supplementary Table S7's 11.38 kPa mean strength remains unresolved.
The supplied evidence does not establish the latest field frontier or whether later work achieved the proposed capability as of November 1, 2026.

The proposed 10 MPa criterion needs a selected nominal-stress area convention and configuration-specific loading protocol before execution; reporting both net material and gross envelope areas preserves the distinction but does not itself select the acceptance convention.
Whether the object must support working loads throughout transformation, and what temporary supports are permitted, remains an application-dependent requirement.
Roster titles permit qualified conceptual comparisons, but full definitions of MEC-08, MEC-10 and the other related entries are needed to verify exact boundaries and shared architectures.
Figures and movies were not visually inspected in the supplied review; interpretation of the demonstrations is limited to the reviewed text and extracted tables.

brief.title: Structures that switch between support and motion
possible: A machine could use the same structural parts as a rigid supporting beam and then as a mechanism with controlled motion. The object would change its internal connections or stiffness—its resistance to deformation—and switch back when needed.
why: Machines could change mechanical jobs while reusing their structural hardware. Equipment could alternate between supporting a load and doing moving work, without exchanging entire mechanical assemblies.

sources.showed: Robots assembled a lightweight lattice, an open framework of connected parts, and demonstrated disassembly and rearrangement. Separate mechanical tests measured the lattice’s strength and stiffness.
sources.quote:
Two types of mobile robots operate over the exterior surface 
and through the interior of the system, performing transport, placement, and reversible 
fastening using the intrinsic lattice periodicity for indexing and metrology.
sources.cited_for: This work demonstrates robotic assembly and reversible changes to a structural framework.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate repeated conversion of the same object between a load-bearing beam and a useful moving mechanism.

sources.showed: Electrically controlled magnetic locks changed how a framework resisted deformation and buckling, the sudden bending that can occur under compression.
sources.quote:
The buckling strength of the structure is altered by an order of magnitude between two
bifurcation states associated with a centrosymmetric and an anti-chiral buckling pattern.
sources.cited_for: Switching internal connections can change mechanical behavior without replacing the material.
sources.not_established: Changing stiffness does not establish repeated beam-to-mechanism conversion with useful load capacity.

sources.showed: Magnetically controlled, spine-inspired beams switched between stiff and flexible states. Combined cells stored mechanical information that could be read visually.
sources.quote: The SRMM exhibits a large stiffness conversion capability (40-fold)
sources.cited_for: Magnetic control provides another route to reversible stiffness changes.
sources.not_established: The stiffness changes do not establish a structure that repeatedly becomes a useful load-bearing mechanism.

sources.who: Zhe Xu, Connor McCann and Aaron M. Dollar
sources.showed: A chain of rigid links with magnetic connectors folded into frameworks approximating different shapes and could be taken apart and rearranged.
sources.quote:
After describing the
concept and design, we demonstrate a prototype consisting of 350
links and experimentally show that objects with different shapes
can be successfully approximated by our proposed chain design.
sources.cited_for: Reusable connected parts can form different structural shapes.
sources.not_established: Different shapes do not establish autonomous switching between a strong beam and a controlled moving mechanism.

shown: Gregg and colleagues demonstrated robots building and rearranging a lightweight structural framework. Haghpanah’s and Lou’s teams demonstrated controllable stiffness changes. These establish parts of the capability: changing a structure’s arrangement or its response to force.
missing: The same object must repeatedly switch between a useful supporting beam and a mechanism with controlled motion.
Both states must carry useful loads while retaining strength and stiffness after repeated transformations.
Power, control and supporting equipment must work together without making the complete system impractical.

milestones.label: A beam repeatedly becomes a useful moving mechanism
milestones.explanation: An object would have to complete 100 autonomous beam-to-mechanism-to-beam trips, with a single independently controlled motion. This would establish reusable mechanical function.

milestones.label: Both states meet the strength target
milestones.explanation: Both states would have to sustain 10 megapascals of force per area, reporting solid-material and whole-section areas alongside stiffness and useful motion. This would distinguish assembled strength from a favorable calculation.

milestones.label: Multiple specimens retain performance through repeated changes
milestones.explanation: Multiple specimens would have to retain strength and stiffness through cycling, with failures, damage, equipment and human help reported in reproducible tests. This would establish repeatability and expose the full system cost.

milestones.label: Transformation costs and operating limits are measured
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to report transformation time, energy, total mass, conditions and support needs, testing any claim of carrying loads during change. This would establish where the demonstrated functions are practical.

uncertain: Must the object carry its working load throughout transformation, or may it be unloaded or temporarily supported?
Which area should determine whether the strength target is met: the solid material alone or the whole section including gaps?
A short cycling test would establish repeatability, but how long would the object retain useful performance?

page.title: Reprogrammable load-bearing mechanical metamaterials
page.definition: A structural object reversibly changes its internal constraints so that the same hardware serves as a load-bearing beam and as a mechanism with one independently controlled motion. Reprogramming changes the motions permitted by the structure, through changes in connections, stiffness or geometry.

goal.need: DARPA proposed reusing one material as a hammer, wrench or screwdriver and specified reversible particle bonds producing elastic moduli of 0.2–4 GPa. Published demonstrations establish separate capabilities: an electromagnetic lattice changed modulus 56-fold; NASA's reconfigurable lattice had a compressive modulus of 1.1129 MPa at 0.0103 g/cm³. These values concern different architectures and loading conditions, rather than equivalent stages of one performance scale.

statements.body: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, Defense Sciences Office
statements.quote: These 3D objects will exhibit all the functionality of their conventional counterparts.
statements.context: BAA 07-21, Addendum 7, published on 25 October 2007, describes objects assembled on command from building blocks up to 1 cm in size.

statements.body: NASA Ames Research Center ARMADAS development team
statements.quote: adapt their properties and form as needed to meet changing needs, use-cases, or environments.
statements.context: The passage describes the intended capability of programmable material systems.

statements.body: Roadmap for animate matter, active mechanical metamaterials contributors Corentin Coulais and Martin van Hecke
statements.quote: combine the flexibility to efficiently do work on their environment with the rigidity to carry a load.
statements.context: Section 15 identifies this combination as a requirement for active mechanical metamaterials.

completion.title: One object repeatedly supports a load as a beam and performs loaded motion as a mechanism.
completion.criterion: One specimen completes two beam–mechanism–beam round trips without replacing structural parts. In each beam state it supports a nonzero external transverse load. In each mechanism state one independently controlled motion delivers positive mechanical work to an external load. The second round trip repeats the same loads, supports and motion range. Unloading or temporary support during transformation is permitted. This establishes the two functions and their repetition; it assigns no minimum strength, deflection limit or fatigue life.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas fallback for the combined capability; no external acceptance test was located.
completion.basis: DARPA's solicitation, NASA's ARMADAS definitions, the animate-matter roadmap, and searches for ISO/ASTM standards and beam–mechanism benchmarks supplied no combined acceptance test. Two round trips are the minimal interpretation of repeated reversible operation. Wu and Pasini already demonstrate structure–mechanism switching; their result does not establish this beam-and-loaded-work test.

milestones.title: A three-dimensional structural material carries both tensile and compressive loads.
milestones.criterion: The assembled material has nonzero tensile and compressive strength. NASA explicitly excludes assemblies of unbonded bricks from its three-dimensional programmable-material comparison. Gregg et al., published on 17 January 2024, tested three hand-assembled 3 × 3 × 3-voxel specimens in compression; the manuscript reports strength of 11.17 ± 0.77 kPa. Those tests establish the compressive component, rather than a measured whole-lattice tensile strength.
milestones.set_by: NASA Ames ARMADAS team, Introduction: scope criterion for three-dimensional programmable materials, rather than a universal metamaterial standard.

milestones.title: A structural material changes configuration after its initial manufacture.
milestones.criterion: The manufactured system physically reconfigures instead of retaining only its initially programmed configuration. Xu et al., published on 9 March 2017, demonstrated different shapes using a 350-link modular-chain prototype. Gregg et al. reported a 256-voxel robotic assembly and a separate disassembly-and-reconfiguration demonstration on 17 January 2024. These establish geometric reconfiguration; neither result establishes the complete loaded beam–mechanism cycle.
milestones.set_by: NASA Ames ARMADAS team, Introduction: published definition of a reprogrammable system.

milestones.title: A metamaterial switches between a rigid structure and a mechanism with one independent motion.
milestones.criterion: Changing internal constraints switches the idealized architecture from zero internal mechanisms to one, excluding whole-object rigid-body motion. Wu and Pasini, published on 10 April 2024, demonstrated this transition in a rotation-square metamaterial using contact-induced hinges. Its compressed specimen was examined in five activation states; each state was tested three times. This establishes structure–mechanism switching, without demonstrating the combined beam-support and loaded-work round trips.
milestones.set_by: The field's kinematic zero-mode criterion, applied by Wu and Pasini in Figure 5. The quoted full-activation condition concerns their rotation-square lattice.
milestones.threshold_quote: the lattice analogy becomes an SDOF mechanism only if there are no red bonds, i.e., the metamaterial is fully activated.

not_found: No independent replication of the complete loaded beam–mechanism round-trip demonstration was located.
The supplied Lou et al. full text remained behind a PMC browser check, and its publisher page returned HTTP 403.
